description.narrative: SUMMARY: Brazil records 500,000 cases per year of sexual exploitation against children and adolescents, occupying second place worldwide. This number can be even higher, since only 7 out of 100 cases are reported. In a context of shrinking civic space and dismantling children's rights institutions over the last 4 years, Plan International Brazil and Ecpat Brazil will join forces in this three-year programme using both a systems and gender transformative approach to combat SEC. PIB will be working from March 2023 onwards to set up a steering committee of youth, enabling vulnerable girls and boys to improve their agency and advocating to combat SEC & gender equality. Moreover, interventions will focus on changing social and gender norms that contribute to the sexual exploitation of children and strengthening, influencing CPS actors (both services providers and LEA) to better implement prevention and response measures and support CSO's movement building to do national advocacy for better CP.

The SUFASEC programme in Brazil builds on the Alliance’s collective achievements to date, scaling up the 2016- 2020 Down to Zero (DtZ), and 2021 – 2022 Building Back Better (BBB) programme. This allows the Alliance to effectively address SEC in the continuously evolving context. Plan International Brazil joined the Down to Zero alliance in the 2016-202 DtZ programme and brought to the country team a rich experience of working with schools, children and youth, local communities, government at local and national level, CSO networks, and CPS actors. Plan International Brazil continues to do so along with a focus on gender transformative programming, a strong understanding of intersectionality and changing social and gender norms.

The key target group (and final beneficiaries) of the programme are girls and boys up to 18 years old, who are victims and survivors and those at risk of SEC. We will mostly work with them through children and youth groups.
Besides this target group, the program will also works with - representatives from private sector - public security officers - actors from the CPS

The programme in Brazil will focus on successful interventions from the previous phases, as well as will build on foreseen opportunities with the new national and state government (ie. Maranhâo). Our main strategy in this new phase is to support CSOs, coalitions, youth organizations and duty bears to strengthen their abilities and create spaces of collaboration in order to improve or create laws and policies. By supporting their capabilities, the project will gain scale at national level and state levels: 1. CSO strengthening and coalition building 2. Meaningful youth participation 3. Social Norm change 4. Duty-bearer engagement 5. Due diligence process with private sector 6. Youth, community and NGO-driven lobby and advocacy The programme has a clear context analysis of SEC in Brazil, showing how and why it affects girls and boys differently, and how and why this is also linked to other exclusion factors, such as race/colour and economic status. During the implementation, activities will tailor media and policy engagements as well as capacity building on key gender norms and barriers/drivers, working on the root causes of SEC, i.e. gender, age, race and economic power imbalances. A steering committee of youth will be created enabling girls from vulnerable and excluded groups to improve their agency, taking action and influencing to combat SEC&gender equality. The committee’s capacity building programme will build increased knowledge, confidence, capacity to speak, to identify and to mitigate risks, to mobilize and to influence others. Boys and young men will also be mobilized as part of the committee to take action on gender equality, in favour of the sexual and reproductive rights realization and against SEC. Finally, the project seeks for an enabling environment, through the provision of capacity building, creating platforms for dialogue and collective proposition, adding efforts to improve coordination among sectors, services and actors and influencing in policies and budget allocations

The programme will work towards the following long-term impact: “Children in all of their diversity are better protected from sexual exploitation.”
This will be reached through three interlinking objectives: 1. Children, youth and their communities successfully challenge social norms and harmful practices related to SEC 2. Children and youth have access to and are supported by strengthened assets and protective environments 3. Children and civil society meaningfully participate in holding duty bearers, including government and local authorities, accountable to their obligations towards improved (implementation of) laws, policies, and systems.
Social norms and harmful practices are key drivers of SEC. Social norm change begins at home, and for children, youth and their communities to challenge these norms, they must exercise high levels of agency and autonomy over their own bodies and lives. To the extent that children and adolescents recognize themselves as subjects of rights, they can also better understand SRHR as fundamental, and both children and youth in general, as well as victims of SEC, can aspire to exercise a healthy sexuality that includes respect for their personal integrity and decisions about their bodies. To the extent that they are recognized as subjects of rights, all children and youth are also able to demand access to inclusive protection services that both duty bearers and co-responsible parties can provide. This agency can be supported through positive parenting, strong family ties and supportive community members. Acting together, children, their caregivers and communities, can achieve meaningful change in how all children engage with and are valued by society.
SEC can be reduced, and its impact appropriately mitigated through access to appropriate assets and through provision of protective environments for children. Economic resilience is a key means of mitigating against monetary drivers of SEC. Children need access to child-centered, inclusive and locally available protection and SRHR information and services, delivered and received without stigma. With so many varied actors involved in protection and referral mechanisms it is important that such services are delivered in a holistic and coordinated manner. By supporting the specialized care and reintegration services that CSOs provide to SEC victims, it is possible to strengthen the restitution of their rights and integrity, especially in contexts where the role of the government in child-friendly and inclusive service provision is still weak.

This activity forms part of the Step Up the Fight Against Sexual Exploitation of Children (SUFASEC) programme. The programme will run in 12 countries in Latin America and South and South East Asia. In Brazil root causes include harmful social and gender norms. The production and reproduction of discriminatory gender norms, sexual abuse and SEC are inherently tolerated and normalized and even encourage the victimisation of children, especially girls, and the perpetration of violence by adults and male peers. Negative social and gender norms interact with weak governance, poverty, income inequality and racism to create an environment in which violence occurs with impunity and is normalised. In the case of Brazil, race - , age- and gender-related social norms come into play regarding sexual violence and SEC. Root causes also include many children’s inability to build social assets that are essential to their protection, families’ economic hardship and exposure to negative shocks such as unemployment, illness or death within the family, or natural disasters. Urbanization and migration can contribute to children’s risk of exposure to SEC, particularly when family separation is involved or where children are migrating for work to support household income needs. Lastly weak governance and child protection systems (duty bearers) do not implement sufficiently protection and response measures in order to protect children’s rights. Especially under the last government civic space has been under pressure and mechanisms (such as the Intersectoral Commission to Combat Sexual Violence against children and Adolecents) have been dismantled. The program will focus on rebuilding these spaces under a newly installed government, advocating for actions that integrate policies for prevention and response of SEC.

Access to protection and SRHR services for adolescent boys is also low, but there are different reasons for this than for girls. The hypothesis is that among boys it is also more strongly related to a lack of sex education, but refers, for example, to a hegemonic masculinity that lays the responsibility for contraception on women and is often also combined with a refusal to use condoms. Therefore, the lack of search for services for this specific group may be related to this aspect.

The integrated work with Health and Social Assistance services has shown positive effects: the percentage of adolescents who reported having a better understanding of their rights after participating in the project’s activities increased from 63% to 94%, while the perception that the project encouraged them to seek health and protection services rose from 59% to 81%. These results demonstrate not only greater awareness, but also a concrete movement toward closer engagement between adolescents and support services, indicating stronger preventive strategies and a greater capacity among young people to seek help in situations of vulnerability, including those related to sexual exploitation and violence

The coordinated work between health and social assistance services has had positive effects on the 44 girls supported by the project. It strengthened their awareness of their rights, improved their understanding of how to access protection and health services, and increased their motivation to seek support when needed. This has enhanced preventive efforts and helped the girls feel better prepared to seek help in situations of vulnerability, including sexual exploitation and violence.

title.narrative: Sexual Reproductive Health and Rights H
# of private sector company policies blocked, adopted, improved leading to decrease of barriers to SRHR and HIV/AIDS services

comment.narrative: Here are no baseline data for this indicator as there was no response to the questionnaires by private sector companies. However we know that in the city of São Luís no approved policies leading to decrease of barriers to SRHR/ or address SEC have been adopted by private sector . Although a few years ago some civil society organisations wrote a code of conduct on prevention of sexual violence , the policy has not been finalised and adopted by any company
Code of conduct or mechanisms in place for private sector companies that address SEC drafted, in the approval phase or approved

In the final year, the project advanced in engaging the private sector through the mapping of companies with the potential to commit to reducing barriers to access to Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) and HIV/AIDS services, while also analyzing their performance and track record in addressing sexual violence against children and adolescents. This process served as a strategic filter to avoid weak partnerships and identify actors with real implementation capacity, resulting in the signing of a technical cooperation agreement among companies, trade unions, and associations. The agreement defined formal responsibilities in tackling sexual exploitation, marking a qualitative advance in institutional practices and establishing solid foundations for the future development of corporate policies aligned with adolescent protection.

title.narrative: # of governmental policies blocked, adopted, improved leading to decrease of barriers to SRHR and HIV/AIDS services

comment.narrative: The State of Maranhao has a range of CP policies and action plans in place, among them the Municipal Plan for Confronting Sexual Violence against Children and Adolescents in São Luís. However, the adherence to this plan has been weak with the previous government giving low priority to children's rights. Currently, the plan is about to expire and the monitoring committee composed of organisations and government actors are not committed to revise and develop the new plan. The Alliance aims to support in the revision of the action plan, promoting both commitment and raise attention fo the reference to SRHR and SEC in particular.

in order to revise the Municipal Plan to Combat Sexual Violence against Children and Adolescents in São Luís, which will expire in 2024, the SUFASEC project will support the re-establishing of the Municipal Committee, which will carry out this review and submit it (the plan) to the Municipal Council for approval. The Alliance will emphasise actions to combat the Sexual Exploitation of Children and Adolescents, as well as Sexual Rights and Reproductive Rights. The context study being carried out will provide important insights for the construction of the municipal plan. The committee is composed by different secretariats, councils for the defence of the rights of children and adolescents in the municipality and civil society organisations.

"The adoption of Resolution No. 47/2025, which establishes guidelines for the Pedagogical Project for Awareness-Raising, Training, and Capacity Building of employees of the Municipality of São Luís, represents a significant step forward. The regulation institutionalizes training practices, ensures the continuity of actions, and strengthens a more structured and responsive policy to address the needs of children, adolescents, and their families.
This resolution provides concrete evidence of improved implementation of Law No. 13.431/2017 in the municipality and constitutes a direct result of the program’s interventions, especially following the dissemination of the context study and the reflections produced by professionals during the training activities offered. These processes expanded understanding of the local reality, strengthened technical capacities, and provided qualified input for decisions more closely aligned with the needs of adolescents in São Luís.
Although the creation of this resolution had already been envisaged, its effective adoption was driven by the program’s actions in coordination with local partnerships and by the reactivation of the Monitoring Committee of the Municipal Plan to Combat Sexual Violence against Children and Adolescents in São Luís, Maranhão, which directly contributed to guiding, prioritizing, and accelerating this regulatory advance."

title.narrative: # of advocacy networks with increased L&A capacities

comment.narrative: The mobilization carried out during this period made it possible to reach 13 civil society and public organizations that began to include in their strategic plans a commitment to strengthening network-based action to prevent and respond to situations of sexual exploitation and violence against children and adolescents (CSEC). These organizations, which are part of the Child-Friendly Network and have recognized political influence in São Luís — including a historic contribution to reducing child labor — demonstrate significant institutional capacity, although they still require technical updating to adequately address the current context of sexual exploitation. The joint work has been strengthened by a strategic replanning process that positioned this mobilization in the third year of the project, creating more favorable conditions for consolidating effective partnerships. In this context, technical meetings are being conducted to identify inclusive spaces for political advocacy, disseminate updated approaches to addressing the issue, and incorporate the active participation of young people, thereby strengthening coordinated action capable of generating more robust, integrated, and sustainable responses for the protection of children and adolescents.

comment.narrative: This indicator includes young people reached with information on SEC (and not only SRH). The current situation in Sao Luis as target region, reach out to youth is limited in and out of schools. The curriculum for CSE is absent, especially after lack of attention for this topic under right wing, conservative power. Also social and gender norms don't allow for an enabling environment to reach youth (female and male) with CSE. At community level, community leaders are very conservatiive and reluctant to address this in community level. Barriers and strategies to reach girls and boys vary related to norms around CSE and roles in society.

The actions planned for the final year were implemented with a focus on training adolescents aged 13 to 18, carried out in public schools and expanded to other partner institutions through peer-to-peer multiplication activities. We used Plan International’s Champions of Change methodology, adapted to the context of the Down to Zero project in Brazil, incorporating specific themes such as CSEC, SRHR, leadership, social participation, and youth activism. This methodological approach made it possible to address gender norms, reflect on cultural and social factors that influence behavior, and strengthen young people’s capacity to recognize and respond to situations of sexual exploitation and violence. The implementation of these strategies directly contributed to achieving the outcome by increasing youth engagement and strengthening preventive actions in the territory.

The training with the youth committee was comprehensive and adapted to local needs, ensuring that young people received comprehensive and relevant information on topics such as: SEC, activism, participation, leadership and SRHR. Young people between the ages of 13 and 18 who take part in the committee have taken part in dialogues and discussions with the protection network. This helps to support the dissemination of relevant information to the young people. In particular, the Champions of Change methodology has helped to strengthen their training process. Young people can use the methodology in face-to-face actions. The young people have been invited by their school managers and partners to take part in awareness-raising activities with other groups of young people, which shows that the for-to-face strategy is effective.
